limitations: Automated accessibility rules cover only part of WCAG; a finding is not a conformance verdict.
A correlated trace shows that a request reached Drupal with the same trace id. It does not show that the patch caused the observed behaviour.
Server timings include tracing and database-logging overhead when instrumentation is on. Do not compare them with a benchmark run.
Drupal page-cache and dynamic-page-cache hits can serve a response without the instrumented request path; those requests may have no server trace.

rows.note: The same scenario can issue a different number of requests, for example after an AJAX response.
Instrumented runs include database-logging and export overhead. A single pair is also noisy; repeat the run before drawing any inference, and treat the difference as diagnostic, not as a benchmark.
Total depends on how many requests the scenario made; compare the median as well.
Cache state and the number of requests affect this. A difference is not by itself a problem.
Query logging measures statement time only; it excludes PHP and rendering.
Inferred from queries against cache tables. This is not a cache hit/miss ratio.
Only exception class and count are recorded; messages are not exported.
Scanner findings, not a WCAG conformance result. Compare only when both sides were scanned at the same step.

comparison.interpretation: Observed data, not a causal claim. A difference in duration, query count or cache activity describes what happened in these two runs under these conditions. It does not establish that the patch caused a performance or functional regression; tracing overhead, cache state, request count and environment differences can all change these numbers. Use the per-request traces and the native browser, axe-core and Lighthouse artifacts to investigate, and re-run without instrumentation before making a performance claim.
